data.content:
Rosetta Stone
The Rosetta Stone is a granodiorite stele bearing a decree issued at Memphis in 196 BC on behalf of King Ptolemy V of Egypt, featuring text in Egyptian hieroglyphs, Egyptian Demotic, and Ancient Greek, and is currently held by the British Museum in London.

Memphis
Memphis is the city where the decree inscribed on the Rosetta Stone was issued in 196 BC.

Ptolemy V
Ptolemy V was the King of Egypt on whose behalf the decree on the Rosetta Stone was issued; he affirmed the royal cult and listed benefits granted to temples.

Egyptian Hieroglyphs
Egyptian Hieroglyphs is a writing system that had been unreadable for centuries until deciphered using the Rosetta Stone, with the deciphering process involving the analysis of its signs and sounds.

Egyptian Demotic
Egyptian Demotic is one of the three scripts found on the Rosetta Stone, occupying thirty-two lines of text.

Ancient Greek
Ancient Greek is one of the three scripts found on the Rosetta Stone, occupying fifty-four lines of text.

Napoleon Bonaparte
Napoleon Bonaparte was the leader of the French military campaign in Egypt during which the Rosetta Stone was discovered in 1799.

Rosetta
Rosetta, also known as el-Rashid, is a town in the Nile Delta near where the Rosetta Stone was found in 1799.

Nile Delta
The Nile Delta is the geographic region in Egypt where the town of Rosetta and the Rosetta Stone are located.

Pierre-François Bouchard
Pierre-François Bouchard was an engineer serving with the French expedition who is generally credited with recognizing the significance of the Rosetta Stone.

Capitulation of Alexandria
The Capitulation of Alexandria was the agreement under which the Rosetta Stone passed into British hands after the French surrender in Egypt in 1801.

British Museum
The British Museum in London has held the Rosetta Stone since 1802, where it remains one of the most visited objects in the collection.

Thomas Young
Thomas Young was an English polymath who made early progress in deciphering Egyptian hieroglyphs in the 1810s by identifying that some signs recorded the sounds of a royal name.

Jean-François Champollion
Jean-François Champollion was a French scholar who announced in 1822 that he had cracked the hieroglyphic writing system, building on the work of Thomas Young.

Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres
The Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres in Paris is where Jean-François Champollion read his letter announcing the decipherment of hieroglyphs in September 1822.

Memphis Decree
The Memphis Decree is the specific text inscribed on the Rosetta Stone, issued by a council of Egyptian priests to affirm the royal cult of Ptolemy V and list benefits granted to temples.

KV62
KV62 is the designation for the tomb of Tutankhamun, discovered in the Valley of the Kings in November 1922, containing over five thousand artifacts including the gold funerary mask.

Valley of the Kings
The Valley of the Kings is the location where the tomb of Tutankhamun (KV62) was discovered.

Howard Carter
Howard Carter was the British archaeologist who led the excavation of Tutankhamun's tomb and discovered it in November 1922.

Lord Carnarvon
Lord Carnarvon, full name George Herbert, 5th Earl of Carnarvon, was the patron of Howard Carter who funded the search for Tutankhamun's tomb and died in Cairo in April 1923.

George Herbert
George Herbert, 5th Earl of Carnarvon, is the full name of Lord Carnarvon, the patron of the excavation of Tutankhamun's tomb.

Tutankhamun
An ancient Egyptian king whose tomb discovery is regarded as one of the most significant archaeological finds of the twentieth century, preserving intact material and insight into New Kingdom royal burial practices.<SEP>Tutankhamun was a pharaoh of the 18th Dynasty who ruled from approximately 1332 BCE to 1323 BCE, son of Akhenaten, whose tomb was discovered by Howard Carter.

Akhenaten
Akhenaten was the pharaoh known for promoting the worship of the sun disk Aten and was the father of Tutankhamun.

Aten
Aten is the sun disk whose worship was promoted by the pharaoh Akhenaten.

18th Dynasty
The 18th Dynasty is the royal lineage to which Tutankhamun and Akhenaten belonged.

Gold Funerary Mask
The Gold Funerary Mask is an iconic artifact from Tutankhamun's tomb, part of a series of three nested coffins, later moved to the Grand Egyptian Museum.

Egyptian Museum
A museum in Cairo that initially housed the artifacts from the tomb of Tutankhamun.<SEP>The Egyptian Museum in Cairo initially housed the artifacts from Tutankhamun's tomb before many were moved to the Grand Egyptian Museum.

Grand Egyptian Museum
A museum located near the Giza pyramids where many artifacts from Tutankhamun's tomb, including the gold mask, were later moved.<SEP>The Grand Egyptian Museum near the Giza pyramids currently houses many artifacts from Tutankhamun's tomb, including the gold mask.

Giza
A location near the pyramids where the Grand Egyptian Museum is situated.<SEP>Giza is the location near the pyramids where the Grand Egyptian Museum is situated.

Cairo
Cairo is the city in Egypt where Lord Carnarvon died in April 1923 and where the Egyptian Museum is located.

Giza Pyramids
The Giza Pyramids are the historical monuments near which the Grand Egyptian Museum is situated.

New Kingdom
A historical period in ancient Egypt regarding which Tutankhamun's tomb provided insight into royal burial practices.

Orville Wright
One of the Wright brothers who piloted the first flight of the Wright Flyer on December 17, 1903, and lived until 1948.

Wilbur Wright
One of the Wright brothers who piloted the longest flight of the first day, conducted public demonstrations in France in 1908, and died in 1912.

Kitty Hawk
A location in North Carolina near the Kill Devil Hills where the first powered flight of the Wright Flyer took place.

Kill Devil Hills
A site in North Carolina known for its sandy dunes, steady winds, and soft sand, used by the Wright brothers for glider testing and powered flight.

Wright Flyer
The first sustained, controlled powered heavier-than-air aircraft, powered by a custom-built engine, with a wingspan of about 12.3 meters and weight of roughly 274 kilograms.

Charlie Taylor
The mechanic who helped the Wright brothers design the custom-built gasoline engine for the Wright Flyer.

John T. Daniels
A local businessman and photographer who captured the famous photograph of the first flight of the Wright Flyer.

data.entity_name: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
data.content:
Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
A museum in Washington, D.C., where the original 1903 Wright Flyer is preserved and displayed.

Wright Company
A company founded by the Wright brothers in 1909 to manufacture aircraft commercially.

Ming Dynasty
A Chinese dynasty that ruled from 1368 to 1644, during which the most visible and best-preserved sections of the Great Wall of China were largely built.<SEP>The Ming Dynasty was a Chinese imperial dynasty that fell in 1644 after the strategic pass of the Great Wall was opened to Manchu forces.

Great Wall of China
A massive defensive network of walls, trenches, and natural defenses in China, largely constructed during the Ming Dynasty using fired brick and cut stone.

Emperor Qin Shi Huang
The ruler who unified China in 221 BCE, a period associated with early wall-building along the northern frontier.

Zhu Yuanzhang
The founder of the Ming Dynasty, also known as the Hongwu Emperor, under whom major wall construction began as defense against Mongol tribes.

Beijing
The capital of China during the Ming Dynasty, near which strategically important sections of the Great Wall were built with fired brick and cut stone.

Badaling
A section of the Great Wall located about 70 kilometers northwest of Beijing, heavily fortified during the Ming Dynasty and opened to tourists in 1957.

Mutianyu
A well-known Ming-era section of the Great Wall first built in 1368 under the supervision of General Xu Da.

Xu Da
A trusted military commander of the Hongwu Emperor who supervised the construction of the Mutianyu section of the Great Wall.

Wu Sangui
A Ming general who opened the strategic pass at Shanhaiguan in 1644 to allow Manchu forces to suppress a rebellion, inadvertently enabling the establishment of the Qing Dynasty.<SEP>Wu Sangui was a Ming general who opened the Shanhaiguan pass in 1644 to allow Manchu forces to suppress a rebellion.

Manchu
A group that established the Qing Dynasty after passing through the Great Wall's Shanhaiguan pass in 1644.

Qing Dynasty
The dynasty established by the Manchu forces after they were allowed through the Great Wall in 1644, marking the end of the Ming Dynasty's rule.<SEP>The Qing Dynasty was established by the Manchu forces after they passed through the Shanhaiguan pass in 1644.

Shanhaiguan
A strategic pass in the Great Wall opened by Wu Sangui in 1644 to allow Manchu forces to enter.<SEP>Shanhaiguan is the strategic pass of the Great Wall that was opened by the Ming general Wu Sangui in 1644.

Li Zicheng
The leader of a rebellion in 1644 whom the Manchu forces helped suppress after passing through the Great Wall.<SEP>Li Zicheng led a rebellion that prompted Wu Sangui to open the Shanhaiguan pass to Manchu forces.

Dayton
A city in Ohio where the Wright brothers ran a bicycle repair and manufacturing shop and built a wind tunnel for testing.

France
A country where Wilbur Wright conducted public flight demonstrations in 1908, leading to widespread international recognition for the Wright brothers.

Washington, D.C.
The location of the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum.

State Administration of Cultural Heritage
A Chinese body that conducted a 2009 survey using infrared and GPS mapping technology to measure the full extent of the Great Wall.

Mongol
Nomadic tribes from the north who conducted raids in the 15th century, prompting intensified construction of the Great Wall of China during the Ming Dynasty.

North Carolina
A US state located near Kitty Hawk and Kill Devil Hills where the Wright brothers conducted their flight tests.

Ohio
A US state where the Wright brothers ran their bicycle repair and manufacturing shop in Dayton.

Nine Frontier Garrisons
The nine defense zones into which the defensive system of the Great Wall of China was organized, each commanded by a regional military governor.

Manchu Forces
Manchu forces were allowed through the Shanhaiguan pass by Wu Sangui and subsequently established the Qing Dynasty.

Great Wall
The Great Wall was a military structure that lost its strategic significance after 1644 but remains a symbol of Chinese engineering and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

UNESCO World Heritage Site
UNESCO World Heritage Site is the designation given to the Great Wall in 1987, recognizing it as a site of cultural importance.

Rebellion Led By Li Zicheng
A rebellion led by Li Zicheng which Wu Sangui sought to suppress by allowing Manchu forces through Shanhaiguan.

Rebellion
Li Zicheng led the rebellion that influenced the decision to open Shanhaiguan.
